options: Accessing memory through a pointer after that memory has already been released with delete
Allocating memory that is never freed
Calling a function before it has been declared
Freeing memory that was never allocated
questions.explain: Use-after-free means the program continues to read or write through a pointer after the memory it refers to has already been deleted — undefined behavior that may appear to work before it fails.

questions.q: Why are memory leaks, use-after-free, double-free, and buffer overruns especially dangerous bugs?
options: They are impossible to detect with any tool
They typically compile without warning and can appear to work correctly for a time before failing or corrupting data silently
They only occur in Python, not C++
They always cause an immediate compiler error
questions.explain: All four bug categories usually compile cleanly and can run without an obvious failure for a while, which is exactly why they're hard to catch without dedicated tooling.

options: It removes all pointers from the compiled binary
It only works on Windows
It instruments the compiled program to detect memory errors like use-after-free and buffer overruns at runtime, reporting the exact offending line
It automatically fixes any memory bugs found
questions.explain: AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) adds runtime instrumentation around memory accesses, so errors are reported immediately with a stack trace instead of silently corrupting memory.

questions.q: How does Valgrind's memcheck differ from AddressSanitizer in how it's used?
options: Valgrind runs an already-compiled binary inside an instrumented emulator, without requiring a special recompile, but runs slower
Valgrind and AddressSanitizer are the same tool with different names
Valgrind can only detect buffer overruns, not leaks
Valgrind requires the exact same compiler flag as ASan
questions.explain: Valgrind emulates the program's execution to track memory accesses, so it can analyze a binary that wasn't specially compiled for it — at the cost of being slower than compiler-instrumented AddressSanitizer.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should sanitizer tools like ASan or Valgrind be run?
options: Never, if the code already uses smart pointers
Only once, right before the final release
Routinely, as part of the test suite, every time the code changes — not only when something already looks broken
Only after a crash has already occurred in production
questions.explain: Because memory bugs can sit silent for a long time before triggering, running sanitizers routinely in CI catches them far more cheaply than diagnosing a live production incident.
